subject: mathb
title: B3 – Power and root functions
outcomesHtml:
The candidate can:

  1. Work with powers (machten): know the special exponents a¹ = a, a⁰ = 1 (a ≠ 0), a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ (a ≠ 0) and a^(1/n) = the n-th root of a (a ≥ 0 for even n), and apply the power rules (rekenregels voor machten):
    • aᵐ · aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ;
    • aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ;
    • (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ;
    • (a·b)ⁿ = aⁿ · bⁿ and (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ;
    • knowing that (a + b)² ≠ a² + b².
  2. Draw and recognise the graphs of the power functions (machtsfuncties) f(x) = xⁿ with rational n, and describe their behaviour: symmetry, vertices and limits.
  3. Use the constant function f(x) = c and the linear function (eerstegraads functie) f(x) = ax + b with its straight-line graph.
  4. Analyse quadratic functions (tweedegraads functies) f(x) = ax² + bx + c:
    • the graph is a parabola with axis of symmetry (symmetrieas) x = −b/(2a);
    • opening upwards (dalparabool) for a > 0, downwards (bergparabool) for a < 0;
    • the number of x-intercepts follows from the discriminant (discriminant) D = b² − 4ac;
    • the vertex is a minimum of a dalparabool and a maximum of a bergparabool.
  5. Use the root functions (wortelfuncties): f(x) = √x = x^(1/2), the inverse of x² for x ≥ 0, with domain x ≥ 0 and range y ≥ 0 (a half sideways parabola), and f(x) = ∛x = x^(1/3), the inverse of x³, with domain and range R.
  6. Combine the power rules with these functions: simplify expressions, solve power and root equations, and compare growth of different power functions.
notesHtml:
B3 — Power and root functions: notes

English notes on the learning outcomes in README.md. Dutch terms are in brackets and italics.

1. Powers and their rules

  • aⁿ is a power (macht) with base (grondtal) a and exponent (exponent) n; n is rational in this syllabus.
  • Special exponents: a¹ = a; a⁰ = 1 for a ≠ 0; a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ = (1/a)ⁿ for a ≠ 0 (so a⁻¹ = 1/a); a^(1/n) = ⁿ√a, the n-th root of a (n = 2, 3, 4, …); for even n both a ≥ 0 and ⁿ√a ≥ 0. In particular a^(1/2) = √a.
  • Rational exponents mix both: a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)ᵐ = ⁿ√(aᵐ).
  • The rules: aᵐ·aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ (add exponents on multiplication); aᵐ/aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ; (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; (a·b)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ; (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ.
  • The classic trap: (a + b)² ≠ a² + b² — there is no sum rule for powers.
  • Roots as powers make root algebra much easier: √x · ∛x = x^(1/2)·x^(1/3) = x^(5/6).

2. Power functions

  • f(x) = xⁿ. For even n ≥ 2: y-axis symmetry, vertex (0,0) is a minimum, y → ∞ as x → ±∞. For odd n ≥ 3: point symmetry in (0,0), increasing through (0,0) with a horizontal tangent there.
  • Negative exponent: f(x) = x⁻¹ = 1/x has vertical asymptote x = 0 and horizontal asymptote y = 0 (see B08).
  • Comparing growth: between two power functions, the one with the larger exponent eventually wins: x⁴ overtakes 100x² for x > 10.

3. Constant and linear functions

  • f(x) = c is the constant function — a horizontal line (it is c·x⁰).
  • f(x) = ax + b is linear (eerstegraads); the graph is the line y = ax + b with slope a and y-intercept b.

4. Quadratic functions

  • f(x) = ax² + bx + c, a ≠ 0: a parabola (parabool), opening upwards (dalparabool) for a > 0 and downwards (bergparabool) for a < 0.
  • Axis of symmetry (symmetrieas): x = −b/(2a); the vertex (top) lies on it and is a minimum (dalparabool) or maximum (bergparabool).
  • The x-intercepts come from the quadratic formula; their number is set by D = b² − 4ac: two (D > 0), one touching (D = 0), none (D < 0).
  • Completing the square (kwadraat afsplitsen) rewrites ax² + bx + c as a(x − p)² + q with (p, q) the vertex: x² + 6x + 5 = (x + 3)² − 9 + 5 = (x + 3)² − 4, vertex (−3, −4). This technique is needed again for circle equations in B13.

5. Root functions

  • f(x) = √x = x^(1/2): inverse of x² for x ≥ 0; domain x ≥ 0, range y ≥ 0; the graph is the upper half of the sideways parabola y² = x; it starts at (0,0) with a vertical tangent and is decreasingly increasing.
  • f(x) = ∛x = x^(1/3): inverse of x³; domain and range R; point symmetry in (0,0).
  • General shifted root functions like f(x) = 2 + √(x − 3): starting point (translated vertex) (3, 2), domain x ≥ 3, range y ≥ 2.

6. Equations

  • Powers: xⁿ = a — see B01 for exact solving and substitution techniques (x⁴ − 5x² + 4 = 0 via y = x²).
  • Mixed powers: x³·x^(1/2) = x^(7/2); x⁵/x² = x³; (x²)³ = x⁶.
  • Roots: isolate, square (check conditions!), verify. A root function can meet a line in 0, 1 or 2 points; after squaring, check every candidate in the original equation.

Worked examples

Fully worked examples for the outcomes in README.md. All examples are original.

Example 1 — power arithmetic

Simplify to one power of x: (a) x⁶ · x⁻²; (b) (x³)²/x⁴; (c) √x · x³ · x^(1/2).

Solution. (a) x⁶⁻² = x⁴. (b) x⁶/x⁴ = x². (c) x^(1/2) · x³ · x^(1/2) = x^(1/2+3+1/2) = x⁴.

Example 2 — vertex via axis of symmetry and via completing the square

Find the vertex of the parabola y = 2x² − 8x + 5.

Solution. Axis of symmetry: x = −(−8)/(2·2) = 2; y(2) = 8 − 16 + 5 = −3, so the vertex is (2, −3). Check by completing the square: 2(x² − 4x) + 5 = 2((x − 2)² − 4) + 5 = 2(x − 2)² − 8 + 5 = 2(x − 2)² − 3. Vertex (2, −3), dalparabool (a = 2 > 0), minimum value −3.

Example 3 — intercepts and discriminant

How many intersections with the x-axis does y = 3x² − 2x + 4 have? And y = x² − 6x + 9?

Solution. First: D = (−2)² − 4·3·4 = 4 − 48 = −44 < 0: none (the parabola lies entirely above the x-axis, as a = 3 > 0). Second: D = 36 − 36 = 0: exactly one, a touching point, x = 3 (indeed (x − 3)²).

Example 4 — root function analysis

Give the starting point, domain and range of f(x) = −1 + 2√(x − 4), and compute f(8) and f(13).

Solution. Start point (4, −1); domain x ≥ 4; the coefficient 2 > 0, so range y ≥ −1. f(8) = −1 + 2√4 = 3; f(13) = −1 + 2·3 = 5.

Example 5 — line meets root graph

Compute the intersections of y = x − 2 and y = √(x + 4) − 2.

Solution. x − 2 = √(x + 4) − 2 ⇔ x = √(x + 4). Square (both sides must be ≥ 0, so x ≥ 0): x² = x + 4 ⇔ x² − x − 4 = 0 ⇔ x = (1 ± √17)/2. Only x = (1 + √17)/2 ≈ 2.56 satisfies x ≥ 0; the other is negative. Then y = x − 2 = (√17 − 3)/2. One intersection: ((1 + √17)/2, (√17 − 3)/2).

Example 6 — comparing growth

For which x > 0 does x³ exceed 10x²?

Solution. x³ > 10x² ⇔ x²(x − 10) > 0. Since x² > 0 for x ≠ 0, this ⇔ x > 10.

questions.questionHtml: Simplify to one power of each letter: (x² y⁻¹)³ · y⁴.
questions.solutionHtml: (x²)³ · (y⁻¹)³ · y⁴ = x⁶ · y⁻³ · y⁴ = x⁶ y¹ = x⁶y.

questions.questionHtml: Find the vertex of the parabola y = −3x² + 12x − 7 and state whether it is a minimum or a maximum.
questions.solutionHtml: Axis of symmetry: x = −b/(2a) = −12/(−6) = 2. y(2) = −12 + 24 − 7 = 5. Since a = −3 < 0 it is a bergparabool, so the vertex (2, 5) gives the maximum value 5.

questions.questionHtml:
a. Write y = x² − 10x + 28 in the form (x − p)² + q and give the vertex.

b. How many x-intercepts does the parabola have? Justify your answer.
questions.solutionHtml: a. x² − 10x = (x − 5)² − 25, so y = (x − 5)² + 3; vertex (5, 3). b. The minimum value is 3 > 0, so no x-intercepts. Check with D: 100 − 112 = −12 < 0. ✓
Need x ≥ 1. Square: 3x + 1 = x² − 2x + 1 ⇔ x² − 5x = 0 ⇔ x(x − 5) = 0 ⇔ x = 0 or x = 5. Only x = 5 satisfies x ≥ 1. Check: √16 = 4 = 5 − 1 ✓. (x = 0 gives √1 = 1 ≠ −1.)

questions.questionHtml: Compute the intersection(s) of the line y = 2x − 3 and the graph of y = √x.

Given f(x) = 3 − √(2 − x).

a. Give the starting point of the graph.

b. Give the domain and range.

c. Describe the shape of the graph (direction of opening, rising or falling).
questions.answerHtml: a. (2, 3); b. domain x ≤ 2, range y ≤ 3; c. lower half of a sideways parabola opening to the left, falling as you move left
questions.solutionHtml: a. The root expression vanishes at x = 2, and f(2) = 3: starting point (2, 3). b. Need 2 − x ≥ 0, so domain x ≤ 2; √ ≥ 0, so f(x) ≤ 3, range y ≤ 3. c. The minus sign reflects the root graph in the x-axis, so from (2, 3) the graph runs to the left and downwards: moving left from x = 2 the root grows, so f falls. It is the lower half of the sideways parabola (y − 3)² = 2 − x, opening to the left.

Factor instead of dividing by x² (which would hide the special case x = 0): x⁴ − 4x² > 0 ⇔ x²(x² − 4) > 0 ⇔ x²(x − 2)(x + 2) > 0. The zeros of the left side are −2, 0, 2; x² is never negative, and (x − 2)(x + 2) > 0 for x < −2 or x > 2. At x = 0 the left side is 0, not > 0. So x < −2 ∨ x > 2.

questions.questionHtml:
The edge s of a cube and its volume V satisfy V = s³.

a. Express s in terms of V.

b. The volume of a cube is tripled. By what exact factor does its edge change, and by what percentage (1 decimal)?
questions.solutionHtml: a. s = ∛V = V^(1/3). b. New edge s′ = ∛(3V) = ∛3 · ∛V = ∛3 · s, so the factor is ∛3 ≈ 1.442, an increase of about 44.2%.
